lines.caption: Every sentence of modern Japanese weaves together three different writing systems.
lines.phonemes: ˈɛvɹi sˈɛntəns ʌv mˈɑːdɚn dʒˌæpənˈiːz wˈiːvz təɡˌɛðɚ θɹˈiː dˈɪfɹənt ɹˈaɪɾɪŋ sˈɪstəmz.

lines.caption: To see why, we have to go back to a time before Japan had writing at all.
lines.phonemes: tə sˈiː wˈaɪ, wiː hæv tə ɡˌoʊ bˈæk tʊ ɐ tˈaɪm bᵻfˌɔːɹ dʒəpˈæn hæd ɹˈaɪɾɪŋ æɾ ˈɔːl.

lines.caption: For centuries, the language of these islands lived only in speech: in conversation, in song, and in memory.
lines.phonemes: fɔːɹ sˈɛntʃɚɹiz, ðə lˈæŋɡwɪdʒ ʌv ðiːz ˈaɪləndz lˈɪvd ˈoʊnli ɪn spˈiːtʃ: ɪn kɑːnvɚsˈeɪʃən, ɪn sˈɔŋ, ænd ɪn mˈɛmɚɹi.

lines.caption: Through centuries of contact with China and the Korean kingdoms, Chinese characters reached Japan, carried by scribes, scholars and Buddhist scriptures.
lines.phonemes: θɹuː sˈɛntʃɚɹiz ʌv kˈɑːntækt wɪð tʃˈaɪnə ænd ðə kɚɹˈiːən kˈɪŋdəmz, tʃaɪnˈiːz kˈæɹɪktɚz ɹˈiːtʃt dʒəpˈæn, kˈæɹid baɪ skɹˈaɪbz, skˈɑːlɚz ænd bˈuːdɪst skɹˈɪptʃɚz.

lines.caption: These characters, kanji, were created for Chinese, a very different language.
lines.phonemes: ðiːz kˈæɹɪktɚz, kˈɑːndʒi, wɜː kɹiːˈeɪɾᵻd fɔːɹ tʃaɪnˈiːz, ɐ vˈɛɹi dˈɪfɹənt lˈæŋɡwɪdʒ.

lines.caption: So scribes in Japan adapted them. Some kanji were used for their meaning. Others were borrowed purely for their sound.
lines.phonemes: sˌoʊ skɹˈaɪbz ɪn dʒəpˈæn ɐdˈæptᵻd ðˌɛm. sˌʌm kˈɑːndʒi wɜː jˈuːzd fɔːɹ ðɛɹ mˈiːnɪŋ. ˈʌðɚz wɜː bˈɑːɹoʊd pjˈʊɹli fɔːɹ ðɛɹ sˈaʊnd.

lines.caption: Written quickly with a brush, those sound characters became softer and more flowing.
lines.phonemes: ɹˈɪʔn kwˈɪkli wɪð ɐ bɹˈʌʃ, ðoʊz sˈaʊnd kˈæɹɪktɚz bɪkˌeɪm sˈɔftɚ ænd mˈɔːɹ flˈoʊɪŋ.

lines.caption: Over generations, the cursive forms were simplified into a new script: hiragana.
lines.phonemes: ˌoʊvɚ dʒˌɛnɚɹˈeɪʃənz, ðə kˈɜːsɪv fˈɔːɹmz wɜː sˈɪmplᵻfˌaɪd ˌɪntʊ ɐ nˈuː skɹˈɪpt: hˌiɾɑɡˈɑːnɑ.

lines.caption: The kanji 安 (an), in flowing cursive, gradually became あ (a).
lines.phonemes: ðə kˈɑːndʒi ˈɑn, ɪn flˈoʊɪŋ kˈɜːsɪv, ɡɹˈædʒuːəli bɪkˈeɪm ˈɑː.

lines.caption: Buddhist monks and scholars, annotating Chinese texts, needed a quicker shorthand, so they often wrote just one part of a kanji.
lines.phonemes: bˈuːdɪst mˈʌŋks ænd skˈɑːlɚz, ˈænətˌeɪɾɪŋ tʃaɪnˈiːz tˈɛksts, nˈiːdᵻd ɐ kwˈɪkɚ ʃˈɔːɹthænd, sˌoʊ ðeɪ ˈɔfən ɹˈoʊt dʒˈʌst wˈʌn pˈɑːɹt əvə kˈɑːndʒi.

lines.caption: The left side of 伊 (i) became the katakana イ (i).
lines.phonemes: ðə lˈɛft sˈaɪd ʌv ˈiː bɪkˈeɪm ðə kˌɑtɑkˈɑːnɑ ˈiː.

lines.caption: Today, all three work together. Kanji carry meaning. Hiragana handle grammar. And katakana mostly write words borrowed from other languages.
lines.phonemes: tədˈeɪ, ˈɔːl θɹˈiː wˈɜːk təɡˈɛðɚ. kˈɑːndʒi kˈæɹi mˈiːnɪŋ. hˌiɾɑɡˈɑːnɑ hˈændəl ɡɹˈæmɚ. ænd kˌɑtɑkˈɑːnɑ mˈoʊstli ɹˈaɪt wˈɜːdz bˈɑːɹoʊd fɹʌm ˈʌðɚ lˈæŋɡwɪdʒᵻz.

lines.caption: 私は日本語を勉強します。 I study Japanese.
lines.phonemes: wɑtˈɑʃi wɑ nˌihˈoŋɡo o bˈeŋkjoː ʃimˈɑs aɪ stˈʌdi dʒˌæpənˈiːz.

lines.caption: Kanji give us "I", "Japanese" and "study". Hiragana supply the particles wa and o, and the verb shimasu.
lines.phonemes: kˈɑːndʒi ɡˈɪv ˌʌs "ˈaɪ", "dʒˌæpənˈiːz" ænd "stˈʌdi". hˌiɾɑɡˈɑːnɑ səplˈaɪ ðə pˈɑːɹɾɪkəlz wˈɑ ænd ˈoː, ænd ðə vˈɜːb ʃimˈɑs.

lines.caption: From temple manuscripts to the screen in your hand, these scripts still carry Japanese culture and identity.
lines.phonemes: fɹʌm tˈɛmpəl mˈænjuːskɹˌɪpts tə ðə skɹˈiːn ɪn jʊɹ hˈænd, ðiːz skɹˈɪpts stˈɪl kˈæɹi dʒˌæpənˈiːz kˈʌltʃɚ ænd aɪdˈɛntᵻɾi.

lines.caption: Nihongo. One language, three scripts, and centuries of history in every stroke.
lines.phonemes: nˌihˈoŋɡo. wˈʌn lˈæŋɡwɪdʒ, θɹˈiː skɹˈɪpts, ænd sˈɛntʃɚɹiz ʌv hˈɪstɚɹi ɪn ˈɛvɹi stɹˈoʊk.
